heading: Area law and PEPS approximation for gapped two-dimensional ground states
lede: Two preprints posted on September 24, 2026 prove an entanglement area law and a polynomial-bond-dimension PEPS approximation for gapped quantum spin systems on the square lattice, assuming only that the full Hamiltonian has a spectral gap. This page tracks the Lean 4 formalization of both proofs.
description: Progress of the Lean 4 formalization of the two-dimensional area law and polynomial PEPS approximation.
label: openai-math

routes.heading: How the area law is proved
routes.intro: The proof shows that any template piece of A shares negligible mutual information with the lattice beyond a sublinear collar around it, and then decomposes A into two families of templates whose entropies cancel.

stages.title: A first bound below volume
stages.physics: Because the ground state Ω is separated from all excited states by a spectral gap, the eigenvalues of a region's reduced density matrix fluctuate little on a logarithmic scale: reweighting Ω inside the region costs energy only where interaction terms cross its boundary. Next, surround a small box with nested regions and place a positive filter operator on each. Choose the filters to maximize the norm {{tn:al-filter-norm}}, where L1, …, Lm are the filters ordered from the smallest region to the largest. Comparing upper and lower bounds on this maximum bounds the conditional entropy of the box: conditioned on its surrounding buffer shells, the box retains at most half of its unconditional entropy{{cite:Lieb1973}} plus a constant times its side length. Averaging this bound over a random ordering of small boxes gives a sub-volume entropy bound.
stages.delivers: For a box of side r far from the cut, the entanglement entropy satisfies S ≤ C r1+e₀, where C is a constant and e₀ is a fixed exponent strictly below 1, improving on the volume bound r².
stages.caption: Entropy bounds for a box of side r on log–log axes, where each power of r is a straight line. The volume bound has slope 2; this stage establishes slope 1 + e₀ with e₀ < 1 (drawn at ½), and the dashed line of slope 1 is the area law reached in the final stage.

diagrams.caption: Lattice sites near a box Q0 far from the cut separating A from the rest of the lattice. The target X is the part of A inside Q0, and the nested regions X1 ⊂ X2 are the parts of A inside concentric enlargements of Q0. A positive filter Lj acts on each Xj, and the shells around X form the buffer.

Proof of Lemma 3.1 as a tensor diagram. For a gapped ground state Ψ with reduced density matrix ρ on a block B, multiplying Ψ on B by F = ρ−u/2 for a small parameter u and tracing out the complement of B produces σ = ρ1−u/M(u), normalized by M(u) = Tr ρ1−u. Because only interaction terms crossing the boundary of B fail to commute with F, the reweighted state has low excess energy, and the spectral gap keeps it close to Ψ. This bounds how far the log-eigenvalues −log pj of ρ deviate from the entropy.

Section 3 staircase filter norm N = ‖Lm⋯L1Ω‖ on the ground state Ω, drawn for m = 2. Positive filters L1, …, Lm act on nested regions X1 ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ Xm around the target X, with shells T1 = X1 ∖ X and T2 = X2 ∖ X1 and exterior Λ ∖ X2. Comparing upper and lower bounds on −2 log N bounds the conditional entropy of X given its surrounding shells.

stages.title: Make the Hamiltonian local and positive
stages.physics: Section 4 replaces the Hamiltonian H by a sum of positive semidefinite operators ki, one per interaction term, each annihilating the ground state Ω: {{tn:al-kill}}. Combining a Lieb–Robinson bound{{cite:Lieb1972}} in the lattice graph distance{{cite:Nachtergaele2006}} with an energy filter whose Fourier transform decays stretched-exponentially{{cite:Gevrey1918}} concentrates each ki near its interaction term, with spatial tails decaying faster than any inverse power of the distance.
stages.delivers: Positive operators ki, one per interaction term, that annihilate the ground state Ω and have stretched-exponentially decaying spatial tails. Their sum is bounded below by a positive constant times H − E0, where E0 is the ground energy, and therefore retains a spectral gap.
stages.caption: Left: the spectrum of H with ground energy E0 and spectral gap Δ. The smooth energy filter χ(E − E0) equals 1 at the ground energy and vanishes on the excited spectrum. Right: magnitude of its Fourier transform at time t on a log scale, decaying faster than any power law so that each filtered term remains concentrated near its support.

diagrams.caption: Construction of the positive terms in Section 4. Given the Hamiltonian H with ground state Ω and ground energy E0, each interaction term hi on support Xi is evolved for time t and averaged against a smooth weight f{{cite:Kitaev2006}} whose Fourier transform χ equals 1 at zero and vanishes on all excitation energies. Subtracting ⟨Ω, hiΩ⟩ yields an operator Mi that annihilates Ω, and the Mi sum to H − E0. Setting ki = |Mi|/c* for a normalizing constant c* gives positive operators satisfying ki ≤ 1.

Section 4 spatial truncation of an operator B to a ball{{cite:Bravyi2006}}. The ball Nl consists of all sites within graph distance l of the anchor site of term i, and “out” denotes the exterior sites. The map Ei,l(B) traces B over the exterior sites and tensors with the normalized identity of dimension q|out|, where q is the local qudit dimension.

stages.title: Replicas trade information against energy
stages.physics: Because entropy is not the expectation value of a linear operator, it cannot be compared directly with the spectral gap on a single copy. The proof therefore passes to k copies of the system. Each copy tensors Ω̃ — the ground state of the Hamiltonian truncated near the target — with a maximally entangled state on two auxiliary registers C and R. Under Schur–Weyl duality{{cite:Schur1901}}, permuting the k copies decomposes each subsystem into sectors indexed by Young diagrams λ, whose normalized log-dimensions converge to the entropy of the normalized diagram. Projecting the R registers onto a single sector λk defines the starting vector {{tn:al-prevector}}, where Bell is the maximally entangled state on C and R and πRλk is the sector projector. Applying an inverse power of a positive operator built from these sectors — interpolated smoothly across a moving partition via trees of matrix geometric means{{cite:Kubo1980}} — converts linear combinations of entropies into an asymptotic log-norm per copy, on which the gap can act. On the symmetric subspace of the copies, a subsystem and its complement carry identical Young diagrams.
stages.delivers: As a small cell moves across the partition, the drop in the replica log-norm bounds the conditional mutual information from above in terms of the energy change. Two estimates then bracket the norm: an upper bound obtained by projecting the target and C onto a maximally entangled state B{{cite:Bennett1993}} ({{tn:al-pin}}, where d* is the Schmidt rank of the pair, z is the mass of the target's typical Schmidt spectrum, and ψ transfers the target's Schmidt index onto R), and a lower bound from the spectral gap showing that a low-energy replica state has most copies in the ground state.
stages.caption: As the number k of copies grows, the log-norm per copy of the filtered k-copy state converges to a linear combination of entropies (dashed). Comparing this limit with the replica energy cost bounds the conditional mutual information.

diagrams.caption: Single-step norm decay in Lemma 5.1 for a pure state θ on four subsystems P, x, U, F. Acting first on x with U and then on x with P, each filter applies the −a/2 power of θ's reduced density matrix ρ̂ on U or P followed by the a/2 power of an arbitrary density matrix τ or σ. By complex interpolation{{cite:Hirschman1952}}, the norm contracts by a factor of e−aη/2 up to higher-order error terms in a, where η is the conditional mutual information of x with F given U (or given P), ℓ = log(e · dim x), and C is a universal constant.

stages.title: Scan a collar
stages.physics: Sweep a partition across a collar Y around the target X along a finite randomized schedule so that each local interaction term is cut in only a small fraction of steps. Applying the replica norm comparisons across this sweep first improves the sub-volume exponent for boxes and then bounds the mutual information between X and the exterior of the collar in the reduced state {{tn:al-collar}}, obtained by tracing the collar Y out of the ground state Ω.
stages.delivers: For a target X = A ∩ T formed by intersecting A with a template T of diameter n and boundary size O(n), and a collar of width proportional to n1−ε with ε = 10−5, the mutual information between X and the exterior of the collar{{cite:Lieb1973}} is at most C n1−ε for a constant C.
stages.caption: Five steps of the sweep around the target (blue). In each step, the partition boundary (orange) cuts through the collar (grey) at a different position chosen from a random schedule, so each local interaction term is cut in only a few steps.

diagrams.caption: Target X, collar Y, and exterior region Λ ∖ S0 on the lattice Λ, where S0 = X ∪ Y. Proposition 9.6 bounds the mutual information between X and Λ ∖ S0 by C n1−ε, where n is the template diameter, ε = 10−5, and C is a constant.

stages.title: Amplify the information bound
stages.physics: Adjoin two reference copies s′ and e′ of the target's sites, swap the target's state into e′, and reset the target to a fixed product state. Projecting onto typical spectral subspaces{{cite:Schumacher1995}} yields an operator that reconstructs the target state together with its purification on s′. Multiplying by random products of the positive local Hamiltonian terms suppresses components orthogonal to the ground state, and polar decomposition{{cite:Autonne1902}} turns the resulting operator into a local unitary U′ near the target: {{tn:al-restore}}, where Ω is the ground state, ρX is the target's reduced state, and triangles denote fixed product states. Because U′ acts only on s′ and sites near the target, without touching e′ or the exterior region, the target has negligible mutual information with the exterior.
stages.delivers: Widening the collar by an additional sublinear width reduces the mutual information between the target and the exterior below any fixed inverse power of the target scale n.
stages.caption: Mutual information leaked past the collar as a function of collar width on a log scale, for a target of diameter n. The collar scan gives the initial bound C n1−ε with ε = 10−5; widening the collar by a sublinear amount drives the leak below n−M for any fixed M.

diagrams.caption: Section 10 amplification geometry. Around S0 = X ∪ Y, the outer region holds all sites within graph distance 2r of S0, with r sublinear in the target scale. The restoring unitary U′ acts only on that neighbourhood and on the reference copy s′, leaving the exterior untouched.

Section 10 Poisson product of local contractions. Each positive local term ki annihilates the ground state, and their sum has gap g. Independent rate-one Poisson clocks on [0, t] apply the contractions Gi = (I − ki)1/2 in time order; their product D fixes the ground state and shrinks the squared norm of components orthogonal to the ground state by e−gt in expectation. Keeping only clocks near the target and truncating each ki makes D local.

stages.title: Arrange regions so the entropies cancel
stages.physics: Remove a boundary set D ⊂ A of size at most a constant times |∂ΛA|, and partition A ∖ D into template regions grouped into two ordered families. A sublinear collar separates each region both from the exterior B = Λ ∖ A and from all earlier regions in its own family. Because the ground state ψ is pure, complementary subsystems share the same nonzero spectrum{{cite:Schmidt1907}}: {{tn:al-purity}}, where Af is one family and A1−f is the other. Narrow buffer strips and local boundary repairs around near-contacts extend the decomposition to arbitrary regions on domains with holes.
stages.delivers: Applying the conditional entropy chain rule once to each family cancels the entropies of all template regions, leaving S(A) ≤ |D| log q (with q the local dimension) plus collar errors bounded by a constant times |∂ΛA|.

diagrams.caption: Two-family cancellation in Lemma 11.1. Inside A lie the excised boundary set D and the templates X1, X2, X3, with X1, X3 in one family and X2 in the other, and B = Λ ∖ A outside. Because each template is nearly independent of B together with the earlier templates of its own family, applying the entropy chain rule to both families cancels the template entropies and leaves S(A) ≤ |D| log q up to summable collar errors.

routes.heading: How the PEPS is built
routes.intro: The construction distributes the ground state among parties, one for each dyadic square, until every lattice site has its own party. Each party may apply arbitrary local maps to its registers and interacts with boundedly many other parties across its lifetime. Compressing the shared pair resources yields polynomial bond dimensions, and routing the resulting links places the tensor network on the square grid.

stages.title: Information fades with angular separation
stages.physics: Two regions have polynomially small mutual information whenever a buffer separates them with width growing linearly away from finitely many corners and staying above a large multiple of log L, where L is the grid side. The proof adjoins cells one by one using the two ordered families of regions from the area-law proof, applying Gaussian energy filtering{{cite:Hastings2006}} across the spectral gap after each step to reset the accumulated error.
stages.delivers: The mutual information between the two regions is at most L−p for any fixed p. Given a partition of the lattice into a region T, a buffer U held by one party, and the exterior E, the owner of U can apply an isometry V{{cite:Uhlmann1976}} that splits the ground state Ω into a product: {{tn:peps-split}}, where s is supported on T and one output of V, and s′ on E and the other output, with error at most √I(T : E){{cite:Carlen2014}}.
stages.caption: Two regions X and E separated by a buffer that narrows linearly toward a corner while remaining of width at least K log L, where L is the grid side and K is a large constant. Their mutual information is at most L−p for a fixed p.

diagrams.caption: Partition in Lemma 6.4 into a region T, a buffer U held by one party, and the exterior E. When T and E have small mutual information, an isometry on U splits the buffer into two registers decoupled between T and E.

stages.title: Small patches with polynomial rank
stages.physics: Near any square of side proportional to log L, where L is the grid side, the ground state lies almost entirely in an orthogonal sum of subspaces, each spanned by a small number of vectors on a nested square tensored with the full exterior space. The nested square may vary from one subspace to the next. Combining nested spectral filters with the spectral gap and the area law bounds the total rank without cutting at a single fixed boundary.
stages.delivers: The internal ranks dj of the subspaces sum to at most C Lc for constants C and c. A local encoder K acting on an outer square Q+ (called a hole) records the subspace index and basis vector into a tag register 𝒥 and resets the interior to a fixed product state, mapping the ground state Ω to the encoded state Ω𝓕: {{tn:peps-encode}}.
stages.caption: Left: nested squares around a patch of side proportional to log L, where L is the grid side. Right: internal ranks dj of the orthogonal subspaces; their sum is at most C Lc, so the subspace and vector index fit in a tag register of polynomial dimension.

diagrams.caption: Around a centre c lie two squares of half-widths h and 2h: Q−(c, h) inside and Q+(c, h) outside (drawn with h = 2). Proposition 4.1 selects nested squares Dj between the two squares, one per subspace j, and the encoder acts only on Q+.

stages.title: Local moves on frames
stages.physics: A frame records which party owns each lattice site and which small squares are stored in encoded form. Three elementary moves modify a frame: changing ownership on a small patch, creating or retiring a party, and swapping ownership of a region between two copies of the state. Creating a party on a region T uses one normalized pair state {{tn:peps-pair}} supported on T and an auxiliary buffer register 𝓑T: the old owner projects privately onto s and prepares a fresh copy of s whose T half is handed to the new party, while all other steps are single-party maps.
stages.delivers: Each patch rewrite changes the target state by at most a constant times L−20, where L is the grid side, and party creations, retirements, and two-copy swaps each cost at most a constant times L−30. These errors sum to a polynomially small bound over the full protocol.

diagrams.caption: Party creation in Lemma 6.5. A party owning a region T and buffer U (with exterior E) applies an isometry V to U{{cite:Uhlmann1976}} with outputs 𝓑T and 𝓑E, projects T and 𝓑T onto a normalized state s, prepares a fresh shared state |s⟩ whose T half belongs to the new party, and applies V†. When T and E are nearly independent{{cite:Carlen2014}}, the error is at most L−30, where L is the grid side.

Two-copy ownership exchange in Lemma 6.6. Two copies of the state, labelled (1) and (2), swap ownership of a region T using only single-party operations: in each copy, the owner of the buffer U applies an isometry V to split off a register 𝓑T paired with T, swaps the T and 𝓑T registers between the copies, and applies V†. The error is at most 4L−30, where L is the grid side.

Small-patch rewrite in Lemma 6.3. The decoder Kold† undoes the old encoding on the square Q+ and its tag register 𝒥old, the projectors P1, …, Pm restrict m nearby patches to low-rank subspaces, and the encoder Knew writes the new encoding and tag 𝒥new. The error is at most (m + rold)ε, where rold counts the modified old squares and ε = L−60 on the grid of side L.

stages.title: A dyadic distribution protocol
stages.physics: Starting from a single party holding the entire ground state Ω, ownership passes down a hierarchy of dyadic squares, halving the square side at each scale until every lattice site has its own party. Ancilla copies of Ω provide the surrounding buffer regions required at each ownership transfer.
stages.delivers: Each party participates in at most a bounded number of operations with other parties, all at its own or an adjacent dyadic scale.
stages.caption: Successive scales of the dyadic hierarchy, from a single root party to one party per site. In each panel, the outlined parent square interacts with its child parties (blue) at the next scale.

stages.title: Compress the shared resources
stages.physics: Although the dyadic protocol uses shared pair states of unbounded Schmidt rank{{cite:Schmidt1907}}, the compression step replaces each pair-state operator |η⟩⟨η̃| in the output density matrix by an average of k random product terms: {{tn:peps-source}}, where Uj and Vj are Gaussian random factors on the two halves and 𝔼 denotes expectation. The sum equals |η⟩⟨η̃| in expectation; choosing k polynomial in the grid side L and using the bounded number of operations per party controls the trace-norm error via Gaussian second-moment bounds{{cite:Reed1962}}{{cite:Isserlis1918}}.
stages.delivers: The trace-norm error is independent of the internal Hilbert-space dimensions of the parties{{cite:Renner2005}}, yielding a tensor-network operator with one node per party and bond dimension polynomial in the grid side.

stages.title: Back to a vector on the grid
stages.physics: Fixing each input leg of the compressed operator network to a single product-basis vector (drawn as a triangle) produces a pure-state tensor network with the same virtual bonds: {{tn:peps-column}}, where σ is the operator tensor at a party and v is the resulting state tensor. Some basis choice yields a normalized state close to the ground state{{cite:Hastings2007}} Ω up to a global phase. Because links connect parties only at nearby dyadic scales, routing each link along a row and then a column ensures that each grid edge carries at most boundedly many links.
stages.delivers: A PEPS{{cite:Verstraete2004}} {{tn:peps-sheet}} with one tensor per site of the L×L grid, bond dimension at most C Lc for constants C and c, and normalized state error at most 1/L.
stages.caption: Links between parent and child parties on an 8 × 8 grid, routed along a row and then a column. Stroke width indicates the number of links crossing each grid edge, which determines the bond dimension on that edge.

diagrams.caption: Grid routing in Lemma 8.2. A parent party Q and its four child parties P sit at fixed centre sites of their dyadic squares, and each link (red) runs along a row and then a column, acting as the identity tensor at intermediate sites. Grouping all link indices crossing a grid edge into a single bond{{cite:Barthel2010}} yields polynomial bond dimension because each edge carries boundedly many links.

stages.title: Models and conventions
stages.physics: Both formalizations share the same definitions: Hamiltonians on finite square-lattice domains (possibly with holes), reduced density matrices and entropies of subregions, the global spectral gap as an operator inequality above a unique ground state, and projected entangled pair states with one tensor Av per site v{{cite:Verstraete2004}}: {{tn:peps-tensor}}.
stages.delivers: Formalized statements of both main theorems with no hypotheses beyond those of the two manuscripts.
